examples.title: “Password Expiring” login page
examples.scenario: You receive an email claiming your password will expire today. It includes a button labeled “Renew Password Now” and asks you to sign in on a “secure portal.”
redFlags: The link destination domain doesn’t match the organization’s real domain
The email uses urgent language and a deadline
The login page requests credentials immediately without any verified context
examples.whyItWasPhishing: The message and page are designed to collect your username/password. The urgency reduces your chance to verify before entering credentials.
examples.whatToDo: Do not enter credentials. Instead, navigate to the official login page by typing the organization’s URL directly or using a trusted bookmark. Report the email.

examples.title: Invoice changed payment instructions
examples.scenario: A vendor invoice arrives with a note: “We updated our bank account for this payment. Please use the attached payment details.” The email emphasizes that payment is needed immediately to avoid penalties.
redFlags: New bank/payment details are provided via email, not through an approved finance process
Attachment or link behavior doesn’t match the vendor’s normal correspondence
examples.whyItWasPhishing: Attackers aim to redirect payments to their accounts by impersonating a legitimate vendor and using urgency and authority cues.
examples.whatToDo: Verify any payment instruction changes through your organization’s procurement/finance verification steps (for example, using known contacts or systems).

examples.title: IT support call-back with OTP
examples.scenario: You get a voicemail or SMS claiming “suspicious login detected.” The message tells you to call a number and provides a step that requires you to provide a one-time code (OTP) for “verification.”
redFlags: You are asked for an OTP or verification code
The message directs you to a phone number provided by the sender
The tone is urgent and discourages independent verification
examples.whyItWasPhishing: OTP codes can be used to complete account takeover. The attacker tries to convince you that sharing the OTP is part of the legitimate verification process.
examples.whatToDo: Do not share OTPs. Verify with your internal IT helpdesk using a known number. Report the message.

examples.title: Targeted message referencing internal project
examples.scenario: A colleague receives an email referencing a specific internal project name and asks them to review a “status update” link. The request includes a brief explanation and appears aligned with their role.
redFlags: The sender is not from an internal or expected domain
The link leads to an external page that looks similar to internal tools
The request asks for action quickly or “before end of day”
examples.whyItWasPhishing: Targeted details increase credibility. The attacker leverages authority/role relevance to reduce suspicion and capture credentials or deliver malware.
examples.whatToDo: Check sender identity and link destination. Verify via internal messaging or direct confirmation. Report the email and avoid interacting with links.
